_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: If the one living in it consecrates it, etc.: for now we assume that the one living in it [the renter] consecrated it.
rashi:a2.1: [“The rent leaves to non-sacred status”:] It seems to me that we do not read “the rent”; rather the text reads: “Since he misused it, it leaves to non-sacred status.” That is, once he benefited from the use of the house and misused it, the house left consecration for non-sacred status, as we learned (Me’ila 19b): there is no misuse after misuse with consecrated items except with an animal and service vessels alone. And he must pay the principal and the added fifth, not rent to the Temple, since anything of the Temple’s, once one has misused it, leaves for non-sacred status, as we say in tractate Me’ila (18a): misuse everywhere means nothing but change, and so it says: “And the children of Israel committed a trespass against the Lord … and served the Baalim”; that is change, which takes it out of consecration into non-sacred status. [Rashi’s reading drops the word “rent” that the Davidson English translates; Tosafot (a2.2) defends it.]
rashi:a3.1: When its rent comes, it shall be consecrated: [he consecrated] the rent, and the house he did not consecrate.
rashi:a5.1: Mishna. One repossesses their property: [those obligated in] burnt offerings and peace offerings. Even though a peace offering atones for [neglect of] a positive mitzva, since it is not an obligation upon him it is not regarded as atonement, and he may come to delay it; therefore one repossesses their property.
rashi:a8.1: Gemara. Of the three of them: a sin offering, a burnt offering or a peace offering, since three offerings are written for him [the nazirite]. And we say in the Sifrei of the school of Rav: “And afterward the nazirite may drink wine” (Numbers 6:20): after a single act.
rashi:a9.1: The burnt offering of a woman after childbirth: since she is not permitted to eat sacrificial food until she brings it.
rashi:a10.1: What is it, that the verse placed it first: that is, what is the reason you said that her burnt offering holds her back? Because the verse placed the burnt offering before the sin offering, as it is written: “She shall bring a lamb of the first year for a burnt offering,” and so on.
rashi:a10.2: But doesn’t Rava say: the verse placed it first for its reading: that it be read first in Scripture, and not that it be sacrificed first; in the chapter Kol HaTadir in tractate Zevaḥim (90a).
rashi:a14.1: Where his fellow separated it for him: this man was obligated to bring a burnt offering, and his fellow came and separated one from his own property for this man’s atonement. And Shmuel says that we require that he inform the one receiving atonement.
rashi:a14.2: From his own: for example, where the court repossesses his property, he must say: I want to.
tosafot:a1.1: In brief: Tosafot ask why the owner who rented out his house may consecrate it here, though it is pledged to the renter. In Ketubot (59b) it is compared to one who says, “This field that I mortgaged to you, when I redeem it, let it be consecrated,” which implies he cannot consecrate it at once; yet in Bava Metzia (73b) Rav Mari bar Raḥel, holding a gentile’s mortgaged house, sold it to Rava, which implies the borrower may sell it. The Ri answers: what exceeds the value of the lender’s money the owner may consecrate or sell at once; “when I redeem it” speaks of consecrating all of it, in Bava Metzia he sold the excess, and here he consecrates the excess, so the renter pays rent to the Temple because the Temple is his partner and neither can separate his share. Some distinguish a lessor, to whom the house returns free when the lease ends, from a borrower, to whom it returns only on repayment, though that does not settle Bava Metzia; and elsewhere a borrower consecrates and sells, and the creditor takes it back from the Temple or the buyer if he has nowhere else to collect, as with a slave made a security, while until then it is sacred and sold. So the lessor can consecrate the house, and likewise forbid it to the renter, and that is the halakha. The Gemara’s question implies the renter cannot consecrate it, yet the Tosefta teaches that if the renter consecrated it, it is consecrated: the renter can consecrate it while it is in his possession, and forbid it to everyone for his term; the question here was only how he could consecrate it so as to pay rent to the Temple. Last, the Tosefta (which Tosafot quote: an owner who consecrated his rented-out field, it is not consecrated until it returns to his possession; a renter who consecrated it, it is consecrated until it leaves his possession, and he pays rent to the Temple) says the lessor cannot consecrate: it speaks where the rent was paid in advance, and our case where it was not, as the Yerushalmi says: a lessor who consecrated, it is consecrated when the rent was not paid in advance; if it was, his words are void. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:a2.1: If he lives in it, he stands in misuse: and even though he did not diminish it, he has misused it, as we learned (Me’ila 18a, beginning of chapter HaNehene): one who derives benefit worth a peruta from consecrated property, even though he did not diminish it, has misused it. And although there is no misuse with what is attached to the ground, as stated in tractate Me’ila, chapter HaNehene (18b), one must say that this passage follows Rav, who says that what was detached and later attached is considered detached, as he said that one who bows down to a house has rendered it forbidden. And in chapter HaNehene (20a) too it cites that statement of Rav, saying there: and since he built them, he has in any case misused them.
tosafot:a2.2: This is how we read: “Since he misused it, the rent leaves to non-sacred status,” and so it is in most books. The meaning is: since he misused, and so on; that is, the rent of the house leaves for non-sacred status, since his fellow [the owner] consecrated the house without his knowing, and he misused it by living in it, and the renter discharges [the rent] by way of [payment for] misuse. But one cannot explain “since he misused, the house leaves for non-sacred status,” as Rashi explained. [The next words are unclear in the printed text; they seem to say that] R. M. pointed to what is taught in the Tosefta of Me’ila (ch. 2): one split wood with a consecrated axe, and his fellow came and split with it, and another came and split with it; all of them misused. And at the end of chapter HaNehene (Me’ila 19b) we learned: there is no misuse after misuse with consecrated items except with an animal and service vessels; that is, inherent sanctity is not deconsecrated through misuse as monetary sanctity is. And an axe is not a service vessel but has monetary sanctity, and it should not be counted as a service vessel on the ground that it brings other things to inherent sanctity; all the more so it does not itself come to inherent sanctity, which is the reason we count other service vessels as having inherent sanctity.
gershom:a1.1: He is obligated to provide him a house: the lessor to the renter, for he cannot say to him, “Here is yours before you,” since it has been demolished. [This explains the end of 20b.]
gershom:a3.1: The one living in it: [the house is] not in his possession.
gershom:a4.1: Since he misused: what he benefited from it.
gershom:a5.1: The rent leaves for non-sacred status: for that reason he is liable to bring an offering.
gershom:a6.1: [Misuse: one who benefits from items consecrated to Heaven, because he takes sanctity out to non-sacred status. For instance, where the one consecrating said:] When its money comes, let it be consecrated; he no longer misuses, since he did not consecrate the house but consecrated the rent.
gershom:a7.1: Those obligated to pay valuations, one repossesses their property: [the treasurer does,] if they delay them, since they do not come for atonement and he will not take care to give them.
gershom:a8.1: [Those obligated to bring sin offerings and guilt offerings, one does not repossess their property: since they are for his own atonement, he is careful to bring them.
gershom:a9.1: Those obligated to bring burnt offerings and peace offerings, one repossesses their property: since they do not come for atonement, and he will be negligent in bringing them.]
gershom:a10.1: Even though he does not achieve atonement: this “atonement” is not atonement in the literal sense; rather: even though they are not accepted favorably until he consents to bring them of his own accord.
gershom:a11.1: As it is stated: “Of his volition,” before the Lord. Even so, one repossesses their property [and coerces him] until he says: I want to.
gershom:a12.1: And likewise you say with regard to women’s bills of divorce: although a coerced bill of divorce is invalid, one coerces him until he says, “I want to,” and it is valid.
gershom:a13.1: Over one of the three of them: [whether over the burnt offering, or the peace offering, or the sin offering, he has fulfilled his obligation]. Therefore, if he shaved over the burnt offering, his property must be repossessed so that he brings the sin offering.
gershom:a14.1: The burnt offering of a woman after childbirth: who cannot bring her sin offering until she first brings her burnt offering.
gershom:a15.1: [Since the verse placed it first: as it is written, “one for a burnt offering and one for a sin offering,” and she will not be negligent with it.
gershom:a16.1: The verse placed it first for its reading: that is, the verse placed the burnt offering before the sin offering for reading it, but not for sacrificing it.
gershom:a17.1: Rather, the burnt offering of a leper: there is no need to repossess his property, as it is taught, and so on.]
gershom:a18.1: A burnt offering requires consent: that is, one who brings a burnt offering must bring it of his own volition.
gershom:a19.1: Where his fellow separated it for him: if his fellow separated a burnt offering on his behalf, [one might think] it need not be separated with the consent of the one who vowed.
gershom:a20.1: From his own: where he separates it from his own property. But when his fellow separates it for him, we might say he is amenable to his fellow giving it for him, and we need not ask him, since he is certainly amenable.
gershom:a21.1: It teaches us: that we need to ask him, since sometimes a person is not amenable, and so on. Therefore we require his consent.
rashi:b1.1: With consent: that he informed the one receiving atonement.
rashi:b3.1: When that is taught: that the owner’s consent is not needed at the time of sacrifice, it is taught because they informed him at the time of separation and he was amenable, i.e., he agreed to the matter.
rashi:b3.2: And when I say: that consent is needed at the time of separation. So Shmuel requires consent at separation and not at atonement.
rashi:b4.1: Disagrees with Ulla: for he says the reverse.
rashi:b4.2: Without consent he has not fulfilled his obligation: evidently we require consent for all of them, and this is difficult for both of them.
rashi:b6.1: The baraitot are not difficult for each other: what was taught above, “The burnt offering or the peace offering of so-and-so is upon me, whether with consent or without consent, he has fulfilled his obligation,” and this last one, which teaches that for all of them, without consent he has not fulfilled his obligation, are not difficult for each other: one speaks of the time of atonement and one of separation, for Ulla as he holds and for Shmuel as he holds.
rashi:b8.1: Even at the time of separation: that he requires consent both at separation and at atonement. And even though this first baraita, which teaches that a burnt offering does not require consent, is a refutation of him, because the answer the Gemara gave above, “Shmuel could have said to you: when that is taught it refers to the time of atonement,” is no real answer. Rav Pappa teaches us, by saying that the baraitot are also not difficult for the amora’im, that Shmuel establishes the first baraita at the time of atonement; by implication, Shmuel does not require consent at atonement, and the answer given above is a real answer.
rashi:b10.2: And he agreed: to give the bill of divorce, and did not cancel the declaration.
rashi:b10.3: Lest you say: presumably he canceled the declaration. Rav Sheshet teaches us that he did not. And he derives the reason from the mishna: for if so, let it teach: one coerces him until he gives it.
rashi:b13.1: Mishna. The appraisal of orphans: a court that goes down to the property of orphans to sell it in order to collect for a creditor appraises the land and proclaims for thirty days: whoever wishes to buy, let him come and buy.
rashi:b13.2: And the appraisal of consecrated property: a treasurer who sells land belonging to the Temple.
rashi:b14.1: Examine it for me: see whether it is good.
rashi:b14.2: That he will be reminded: the householder, in the evening, of what he said to the workers in the morning.
rashi:b14.3: And ask them: whether it is good.
rashi:b16.1: Such is its quality: it produces such-and-such an amount of grain.
rashi:b16.2: Such is its appraisal: at such-and-such the court appraised it.
rashi:b16.3: And let him buy on condition: that he pay the wife or the creditor.
rashi:b17.1: Why do I need: to proclaim “in order to give,” and so on.
rashi:b17.2: Bit by bit: little by little. And there is a buyer who prefers to pay a creditor, who is lenient with dinars, accepting broken and deficient coins, since merchants do not usually mind that.
tosafot:b3.1: Shmuel could have said to you: when that is taught, it refers to the time of atonement (and the baraita is dealing with the time of separation). And if you say: why does he disagree with Ulla? Let us set Shmuel’s statement at the time of atonement and the baraita at the time of separation, and he would not disagree with Ulla. One can say: the Gemara holds that Shmuel is speaking of the time of separation, as he is commenting on the mishna, which implies it deals with the time of separation, since it says of those obligated to bring burnt offerings that one repossesses their property [the printed Tosafot read “does not repossess”], and that happens at the time of separation.
tosafot:b8.1: What is “at the time of separation” that Shmuel said? Even at the time of separation: and if you say: they disagree in any case, for according to Shmuel it requires consent even at the time of separation, and all the more so at the time of atonement, while according to Ulla it requires consent only at the time of atonement and not at the time of separation? One can say: in any case, they would not disagree in the way they disagree now. And the Ri thinks the reasoning of Shmuel and Ulla is this. Shmuel says burnt offerings and peace offerings require consent at the time of separation because a person is not amenable to achieving atonement with something that is not his; but at the time of atonement they do not need it, since for the sake of the laying of hands his consent is not needed, as they do not come to atone for his sin. But a sin offering and a guilt offering, which come for a sin and require confession at the laying of hands, require consent at the time of atonement. And Ulla holds that even with burnt offerings and peace offerings a person wants to fulfill the mitzva of laying of hands, so we require his consent at the time of atonement; but at the time of separation consent is required only for a sin offering, because a person is not amenable to atonement with something that is not his, whereas burnt offerings and peace offerings, which do not come for atonement to that degree, need no consent at the time of separation.
tosafot:b9.1: One who delivered a declaration about a bill of divorce, his declaration is a declaration: (a ruling). Therefore people are accustomed to cancel every declaration, and declarations within declarations, at the time the bill of divorce is written and at the time it is given, since we are concerned lest [an earlier declaration] invalidate it.
tosafot:b13.1: Mishna. The appraisal of orphans, thirty days: and if you say: why does it mention orphans? Even with anyone, if the court came to go down to their property to pay a wife her marriage contract or a creditor his debt, a court appraisal of thirty days is needed, as stated in chapter HaMafkid (Bava Metzia 35b): from when may he eat the produce? From when the days of proclamation are completed. Evidently anyone whose property is gone down to requires a court appraisal. If so, why mention orphans? One can say: the tanna taught orphans as a novelty: lest you say orphans should be like consecrated property and require a court appraisal of sixty days, it teaches us that they are like everyone else.
tosafot:b15.1: At the time the workers go out and at the time the workers come in: meaning, at the time the workers go out from their work, and at the time they come in to their work. [So Tosafot read it, the reverse of the Davidson English; Rabbeinu Gershom reads it the same way.] And this is not the order of the mishna, which said “in the morning and in the evening,” while Rav Yehuda explains the evening first and then the morning. One can say: that is the right order, because he does not want to take them from their work, so it is not usual to say “Examine it for me” to them [while they work]. For otherwise, why wait until the evening to ask them what they saw? He is free to ask them all day. Therefore Rav Yehuda needed to explain it so: when they leave their work, he says to them, “Examine it for me,” since then he does not take them from their work; and the next day, when he remembers what he told them the evening before, he goes to ask. And therefore one should not explain the reverse, at the time the workers go out of their homes and enter their work and at the time they come into their homes and leave their work, because that is not the usual way, as we explained; and furthermore, the wording of the text cannot be reconciled with that. In the Tosafot I wrote at great length on this, and they cited the passage at the beginning of HaSokher et HaPoalim (Bava Metzia 83a–b): Rav Asi said: a worker’s coming in is on his own time, and his going out is on the employer’s.
tosafot:b16.1: Such is its quality: for producing grain and fruit; such is its appraisal: at such-and-such a sum. And if the lender wants to keep it at what the court appraised, there is no need to proclaim; rather, we place it in the lender’s hand at once.
gershom:b1.1: [With consent, he has fulfilled his obligation: if he sacrificed it with the consent of the one obligated, the one obligated has fulfilled his obligation.]
gershom:b2.1: Shmuel could have said to you: when that is taught: that for a burnt offering, whether with consent or without consent, he has fulfilled his obligation.
gershom:b3.1: At the time of atonement: it does not need consent, since he was amenable at the time of separation, which was with his consent; surely he is still amenable to that burnt offering.
gershom:b4.1: [And when I say that a burnt offering requires consent, it is at the time of separation.
gershom:b5.1: This and that: both a sin offering and a burnt offering.
gershom:b6.1: Shmuel establishes it at the time of separation: where they did not distinguish; and Ulla [establishes it] at the time of atonement.
gershom:b7.1: The baraitot are not difficult for each other: the first, which teaches that whether with consent or without consent he has fulfilled his obligation, refers to the time of separation. The amora’im, Ulla and Shmuel, certainly disagree.]
gershom:b8.1: Even at the time of separation: that is, at the time of atonement as well, and that is Ulla’s view.
gershom:b9.1: And even though this first baraita is a refutation of him: where it said that whether with consent or without consent he has fulfilled his obligation, which we established as referring to the time of atonement.
gershom:b10.1: It teaches us: that he spoke of the time of separation alone. [And certainly] they disagree.
gershom:b11.1: One who delivered a declaration about a bill of divorce: they were forcing him to give a bill of divorce, and he said to witnesses: Be witnesses that I am being forced.
gershom:b12.1: His declaration is a declaration: and it is not a bill of divorce.
gershom:b13.1: It is necessary only where they coerced him after the declaration, and he agreed, kept silent, and gave it in silence.
gershom:b14.1: Lest you say: since he gave it, he canceled his declaration.
gershom:b15.1: It teaches us: that he did not.
gershom:b16.1: For if so: that giving it without comment is enough, let it teach: one coerces him until he gives it. What is “until he says”? It teaches us that he must cancel his declaration and say: I want to.
gershom:b17.1: We will return to you, HaOmer Mishkali.
gershom:b18.1: The appraisal of orphans, thirty days: when the court needs to sell from the property of orphans, whether for their sustenance or for a marriage contract or for anything else, it must appraise it and proclaim for thirty days [in the morning and in the evening], as the Gemara explains: one says, the field of so-and-so, by its markers and by its borders, such is its quality and such is its appraisal; so that people will hear and come to buy, and each will add to his fellow’s offer.
gershom:b19.1: And the appraisal of consecrated property [sixty days]: when they wish to redeem a consecrated field.
gershom:b20.1: At the time the workers go out: in the evening, when the workers leave their work, one proclaims, so that the householder will hear and say to [the workers]: Go, examine it for me.
gershom:b21.1: And at the time the workers come in: one also proclaims in the morning, so that the householder will remember what he said to the workers the night before, and ask them whether they saw it and how good it is.
gershom:b22.1: [The field of so-and-so, such is its quality, so many kor it produces, and such is its appraisal: that is, at such-and-such a sum the court appraised it.]
gershom:b23.1: For there are those who prefer: to buy in order to give [its price] to a creditor, who is lenient with dinars; for one who pays [a creditor] is not given much chance to check the dinars, as people say to him: “From your bad debtor, take even bran in payment.”
gershom:b24.1: And there are buyers who prefer to give the price to a wife, because she takes it bit by bit, whenever she needs to spend, and not all at once.
